title.en: The Draugr Glamr: Grettir and the Ghost That Waits in the Valley
title.zh: 屍鬼格拉姆：格雷蒂爾與盤踞谷中的亡魂

region.zh: 冰島瓦特恩斯谷（格拉姆作祟之地）

texts.period: Grettis saga 14th century (events set c. 1000-1030); principal MSS 14th c.

source.work: Grettis saga Asmundarsonar chs. 32-35; ed. Islenzk Fornrit VII (1936); English: The Story of Grettir the Strong, Morris & Magnusson

texts.license: Public domain (Morris & Magnusson translation); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: A Swedish shepherd named Glamr works for a poor valley farm, despises the Christian observances, and dies in a blizzard on the mountain. He comes back: his corpse is monstrous, and as a draugr - a walking dead - he rides the roofs, kills men and livestock, and drives the household to the point of abandoning the farm. Grettir, the outlaw strongman, comes to fight him by lamplight; Glamr's dying curse ('I have so fixed my eyes on you that you shall have less fortune from this') falls on Grettir with the ghost's death: he sees the dead man's staring eyes, becomes afraid of the dark for the rest of his life, and his career of exile begins. The record is the saga-world's doctrine of the wrongfully dead: not a myth of gods but of what a corpse does when its owner dies bad-tempered and unblessed.
summary.zh: 瑞典牧羊人格拉姆受僱於貧困山谷農莊，蔑視基督教儀禮，最終死於山間風暴。他死後復歸：屍身龐大如魔，化作屍鬼（draugr）在屋頂馳行，殺人畜無數，逼得莊園主人幾欲棄地。亡命強人格雷蒂爾前來對決，就著燈火與之搏鬥；格拉姆臨死的詛咒——「我已用目光把你盯住，你此後福分必減」——隨屍鬼之死而落在格雷蒂爾身上：他望見亡者圓睜的雙眼，從此畏懼黑暗，放逐生涯自此開始。此記錄是薩迦世界對「不得其死」者的教義：非諸神之神話，而是性情乖戾、未經祝聖的屍體將如何行事。

texts.canonical_translation: William Morris and Eirikr Magnusson, The Story of Grettir the Strong, 1869 (public domain); ed. Islenzk Fornrit VII

narrative.en:
The saga's ghost-story is precise about the making of a draugr. Glamr is a foreign laborer, big, ill-tempered, and - the crucial detail - he despises the Christian observances and will not fast on Christmas Eve; the household goes to mass, and Glamr stays out with the sheep in the snow. In the morning he is found dead on the ridge, 'blue as hell'? - swollen and blackened, staring; and the folk who try to move the corpse cannot, though the priest succeeds only with prayer. The burial goes wrong: the body is laid in a cairn, and that night the farm's troubles begin. Glamr rides the roofs at night, treads the pathways with feet that break the frost; he kills animals and men; he breaks Grettir's? - no, he first kills a serving-man and a shepherd and another laborer, 'so that the people were in despair'. The valley empties: the last household remaining is the one that hired Glamr.

Grettir arrives to fight. The saga stages the duel with liturgical precision: Grettir enters at dusk, hides, and the ghost comes at midnight - 'Glamr came to the door and gave it a great wrench, so that every timber cracked'. The fight is nocturnal, inside the hall, in the lamplight; the draugr's strength is monstrous, and as Grettir breaks him - grips him from behind, wrenches his neck - Glamr speaks the dying words of a draugr: 'you have been bold against me, and it is no wonder; but this is my will: I have so fixed my eyes on you that you shall have less fortune from this; and this of your strength shall depart' - and Grettir, looking down, sees the terrible blue eyes fixed on him, and the saga says 'he never dared go into the dark after that, and he feared the dark? ' - he could not endure darkness alone. The ghost's death is his victory; its stare is his sentence.

The record's cultural functions are a taxonomy of the restless dead and a doctrine of social death. The draugr is not a demon: it is a person who died in the wrong manner (struck by the mountain, unblessed, bad-tempered), carrying its biography into the corpse; the sagas' draugar are consistently the dead of grudges - fighters, misers, outlaws - and their haunting is a continuation of their conduct. The ghost's economy is also social: a draugr destroys a farm's viability, and the legal response is real (outlawry, enforced settlement, church-consecrated ground); Glamr's case is resolved only when he is moved to consecrated ground. And the curse-theology is the saga's sharpest datum: the dying stare is contractual - Grettir's fear of the dark is a contract Glamr wrote with his eyes, and the hero's later career (the burning at Drangey, the lonely island) is the curse's schedule carried out.

In the atlas, the record anchors the restless-corpse family (the Chinese jiangshi, the Mesopotamian etemmu, the Haitian zonbi): each tradition's doctrine of the dead who walk; the Norse draugr is distinctive in being a continuation of personality (bad temper included) rather than a possession, and in being legally actionable - the sagas treat hauntings as property disputes.

functions: Taxonomy of the restless dead: the draugr as a corpse continuing its owner's biography
Social-death doctrine: hauntings as property disputes, resolvable by law and consecrated ground
Contractual curse: the dying stare as a binding schedule on the survivor
Christianity's role in the taxonomy: unblessed, unfasted death as the making of a ghost

The body was laid in a cairn; but that night Glamr rode the roofs, and men and beasts died one after another, until the valley was empty of households.

And Grettir looking down saw the terrible eyes, and never after dared go into the dark alone.

title.en: The Ghost-Court of Froda: The Dead Who Held a Thing
title.zh: 弗羅達的鬼魂議會：亡者自設庭議

region.zh: 冰島斯奈山半島弗羅達農莊

texts.period: Eyrbyggja saga 13th-14th century (events set c. 1000); principal MSS 14th c.

source.work: Eyrbyggja saga chs. 50-54 (the Froda hauntings); ed. Islenzk Fornrit IV (1935)

texts.license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: After a ship's crew drowns in the winter sea, the drowned come home - to the farmhouse, to the fire, to the benches. The dead of Froda multiply: drowned sailors sit by the fire each evening as if alive; then other dead join them, quarrelers and killers, until the ghosts convene each night in the hall and hold their own court (they 'sat in judgment', setting men apart for death); the living are pressed out of their own house. The haunting ends only when a fire is built in the hall and the dead are burned out - and when the smoke clears, the ghosts 'went away as if driven by wind'. The record is the saga-world's most political supernatural narrative: even the dead hold assemblies, and the resolution of a haunting is jurisprudential - burn the court out.
summary.zh: 一船水手葬身冬季大海之後，溺亡者「回了家」——回到農舍、火邊與長凳。弗羅達的亡者日增：溺死的船員每晚如常人般坐在火旁；其後又有其他亡者加入，爭吵者與殺人者相繼而至，最後鬼魂們每夜在大廳集會，自設庭議（「他們坐而論斷」，為死亡點名），生者竟被擠出自己家門。這場鬧鬼唯有在大廳生火、將亡者焚出方能了結——煙散之後，鬼魂「如被風吹散般離去」。此記錄是薩迦世界最具政治色彩的超自然敘事：連亡者也會集會，而驅鬼的方式竟是司法性的——把法庭燒掉。

texts.canonical_translation: Eyrbyggja saga, Islenzk Fornrit IV, Reykjavik 1935; paraphrase

narrative.en:
Eyrbyggja saga's Fróðá episode is the saga corpus's masterpiece of collective haunting. It begins with economics: two ships' crews winter at the farm, and one is drowned when their boat is lost in the winter surf. The drowned men 'came home' the same evening - eighteen drowned men sat in the hall by the fire that night, dripping and silent, 'and folk durst not speak to them'? - the saga says they came each evening and sat as if alive, and the household could not drive them out. Then a second crew drowns; more dead come; and among them arrive the dead of grudges - the burned killer Thórólfr? - the saga's sequence: the dead Thorstein's? - the hauntings escalate from strangers at the fire to killings in the dark: a shepherd is found dead by the cow-sheds, then another, and the living cannot say who kills.

The escalation is political. The ghosts begin to convene: 'they came into the hall every night and sat by the fire? ' - the saga's great scene is that the dead 'held a court': each night they sat in judgment, 'and they sat there, nine on each bench', and they set apart men for death, 'as it were at a Thing'; the household's own dead kinsmen were among them, and their judgments were executed by the deaths that followed. The living, squeezed out of their own hall, finally leave it to the dead - until Snorri goði (the saga's legal hero, also of Helgafell) is sent for. His solution is jurisprudential and material at once: 'let a fire be built in the hall'? - the saga says he advised that the dead be summoned to a legal settlement (a sétta-mál), and that a fire be built in the hall, and the ghosts burned out; and when the great fire is lit in the hall where the ghosts hold court, the dead are consumed? - 'and all the dead men that were in the hall went out as if driven by wind', and the hauntings cease. The dead are then dug up and moved to consecrated ground.

The record's cultural functions are a political theory of the dead and the doctrine that hauntings are litigable. The saga's dead are not chaotic: they organize, convene, judge and execute - the ghost-court is the mirrored Thing of the living, and its existence is the saga's argument that assemblies (not spirits) are what needs governing in this society. The resolution is correspondingly legalistic: the ghosts are not exorcised by ritual but by a combination of legal settlement and fire - a property-dispute solution, consistent with the sagas' treatment of all social problems. And the conversion-era frame is explicit: the dead are finally moved to church-consecrated ground, so the episode is staged as the moment when the old dead accept the new jurisdiction.

In the atlas, the record anchors the mass-haunting family (the Chinese 'haunted yamen' records, the Mesopotamian plague-house incantations, the Japanese yūrei crowds): each a collective haunting narrative; the Norse one is unique in making the haunting an assembly and its resolution a trial by fire.

functions: Political theory of the dead: ghosts convene their own court, mirroring the living Thing
Doctrine of litigable hauntings: resolution by legal settlement plus fire
Conversion-era jurisdiction: the old dead moved to consecrated ground
Mass-haunting as social emergency: the living expelled from their own hall

title.en: Hel: The Half-Dead Goddess of the Ordinary Dead
title.zh: 海爾：凡俗亡者的半死女神

region.en: Hel's hall, Niflheim (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 尼福爾海姆海爾之廳（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

texts.period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230 (older material); Voluspa st. 31 allusion; Lokasenna st. 32-33; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, GKS 2365 4to

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 34; Lokasenna st. 32-33; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

texts.license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Hel is Loki's daughter by the giantess Angrboda: cast down by Odin into Niflheim, she is given authority over nine worlds 'to apportion abodes to those sent to her'. Her body is the doctrine: half flesh-colored and alive-looking, half blue-black and dead; her face is 'more downcast and fierce' than others'. Lokasenna confirms her office in Loki's own taunt: it was Hel's hand that took the ring Draupnir from Baldr's pyre? - no: Loki says Odin laid the ring on the pyre and Hel received it; her power is the power to receive. The record is the Norse personification of the ordinary death: a goddess who is herself half-dead, ruling the unchosen majority.
summary.zh: 海爾是洛基與女巨人安格爾波達之女：被奧丁貶入尼福爾海姆，獲掌九界之權，「為被遣至她處者分配居所」。她的身體即是教義：半邊肉色似生者，半邊青黑如死者；其面容「比他人更陰鬱凶厲」。《洛基的吵罵》中洛基親口證實她的職能：奧丁將德羅普尼爾指環放於巴爾德火葬堆，由海爾收下——她的權力便是「收下」。此記錄是北歐對「尋常之死」的人格化：一位自身半死的神，統轄未經挑選的眾多亡者。

texts.canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning introduces Hel in the same chapter as her brothers, and her portrait is the shortest but the most complete. Loki had three children by Angrboda: Fenrir the wolf, Jormungand the serpent, and Hel - 'a girl'. When the gods learn what a brood is being reared in Jotunheim, the All-father sends messengers to bring them to him; the serpent he throws into the sea, the wolf he binds, and Hel he 'cast down into Niflheim', giving her authority over nine worlds, 'that she should apportion all abodes to those that were sent to her': this is Hel's realm, the ninth world, where the dead of sickness and age go. Her body is a cosmological diagram: 'half of her is blue-black and half flesh-colored, and she is easily known; and, further, she is more downcast and fierce-looking than the others'. The half-body reads the realm: living side up, dead side down; the gods' world above, the dead's below.

The eddic poems give her the office's flavor. In Lokasenna's flyting, Loki - her own father - taunts Frigg with the fact of Baldr's stay in Hel and praises her realm as obedient: 'Be silent, Frigg... thou hast ever been mad after men; because? ' - and, of the ring: 'Odin's son set the ring on Baldr's pyre; and Hel received it' - the goddess as the receiver of gifts, the custom-house of the dead. In Hyndluljod's genealogical litany she is 'Hel' among Loki's family, and Baldrs draumar's geography shows her court in action (the benches strewn for Baldr, the mead brewed). Her rulership is administrative rather than moral: she is not a judge, and Nastrand's punishments are a separate doctrine; her power is custody.

The record's cultural functions are the personification of ordinary death and the doctrine of the half-body. Norse myth has no god of the grave-buried war-hero (that is Odin's office) and no god of the drowned (Ran's); Hel is the personification of the majority death, and her body's split is the myth's way of saying that she herself stands on both sides of the border - a goddess who has never been alive and cannot fully die. The name gave English 'hell' through Christian reception, and the semantic history is a critical-digital-history datum in itself: the same word, meaning the gray household of the ordinary dead, was re-lexicalized as the place of punishment; this record preserves the older referent.

In the atlas, Hel answers the Greek Hades (the personified realm-ruler), the Mesopotamian Ereshkigal, and the Japanese Yomi's Izanami - each a death-personification; the Norse one is distinctive in being half-dead in body, female, and the child of the trickster rather than of the first gods.

functions: Personification of the ordinary death: ruler of the majority dead, without moral judgment
Half-body doctrine: the goddess herself split between living and dead sides
Custody office: the receiver of the dead and of the pyre-gifts
Semantic-historical datum: 'Hel' as the older referent of the word later meaning 'hell'

title.en: Thokk's Refusal: The One Dry Eye That Kept Baldr in Hel
title.zh: 索克的拒絕：唯一乾涸的眼睛，讓巴爾德長留冥府

region.en: The world-wide weeping and one cave in Jotunheim (symbolic pin at Jotunheimen, Norway)
region.zh: 普世哭泣與約頓海姆一處洞穴（象徵性定位於挪威尤通黑門山）

texts.period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230 (older material); principal MS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 49; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

texts.license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: To ransom Baldr from Hel, the gods send messengers through all worlds asking everything to weep him alive: men, animals, earth, stones, trees, metals - all consent. Only in a cave sits a giantess who names herself Thokk ('thanks'), dry-eyed, and refuses: 'Neither quick nor dead needed I Baldr's weeping? - let Hel hold what it has.' And she is Loki in disguise. One refusal voids the unanimous contract, and Baldr stays in Hel until the world's renewal. The record is the Norse doctrine that resurrection requires total participation: a single withholding defeats a universe's grief.
summary.zh: 為將巴爾德從海爾手中贖回，諸神遣使遍歷諸界，請求萬物為之哭泣：人類、鳥獸、大地、石頭、樹木、金屬——無不應允。唯有一洞穴中坐著一位自稱「索克」（「謝意」）的女巨人，眼中無淚，拒絕哭泣：「無論生死，我不需要巴爾德的眼淚——讓海爾留著她已有的吧。」而她正是喬裝的洛基。一個拒絕便作廢了全體一致的契約，巴爾德遂長留冥府，直至世界更新。此記錄是北歐的教義：復生需要全體參與——一滴不肯落下的眼淚，足以擊敗整個宇宙的悲傷。

texts.canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The weeping-transaction is the myth's most legalistic scene. After Hermothr returns with Hel's terms - Baldr shall ride home if all things weep for him - the Aesir send messengers 'through all the world' to bid everything weep Baldr out of Hel: 'and all things did - men and every living creature, and the earth, and the stones, and the trees, and all metals, just as you will have seen these things weep when they come from frost into heat'. The list is the myth's phenomenology of thaw: dew on stones, sap in trees, moisture on metal - the world's own weeping, cosmic and material. The doctrine beneath it is that resurrection is a unanimity-contract: the underworld releases only what the whole cosmos mourns.

The contract's one dissent is the myth's sharp end. The messengers 'came at last to a certain giantess, who called herself Thokk', sitting in a cave; she refuses: 'Thokk will weep dry tears for Baldr's burial; neither quick nor dead got I any joy of him? - let Hel hold what it has.' Snorri then unmasks her: 'men believe that this same Thokk was Loki, Lopt's son, who has most? ' - no: 'who all? ' - the text: 'and men believe that she who refused was Loki himself'. The giantess's name is a pun - thokk, 'thanks', as if the refusal were a courtesy - and the disguise is the trickster's signature: the cosmos's unanimous grief defeated by a cross-dressing father's courtesy.

The record's cultural functions are the unanimity-doctrine of resurrection and the trickster's veto. Where most mythologies make death's reversal a matter of ritual or heroism, the Norse makes it a matter of total assent - a social contract with a death-clause; and the myth's history of its failure is a portrait of the trickster as the one agent able to withhold consent: gods, stones, trees and metals all weep, but the father who engineered the death wears a woman's shape and declines. The record also closes Baldr's arc: he stays in Hel 'until the renewal', when 'Baldr and Höd shall come back' - the failed ransom and the scheduled return are one doctrine: death cannot be bought back piecemeal; it can only be outlived.

In the atlas, the record anchors the withheld-consent family: the Greek Orpheus' glance, the Inanna-returns-with-a-substitute doctrine, the Japanese Izanagi's turn back - each a resurrection defeated at a single exit-condition; the Norse one is distinctive in locating the failure not in the rescued or the rescuer but in the universe's one dissenter.

functions: Unanimity-doctrine of resurrection: release requires the whole cosmos's weeping
Phenomenology of thaw: the world's own moisture as the weeping
Trickster's veto: one disguised refusal defeats universal grief
Closes Baldr's arc: failed ransom, scheduled return at the renewal

passages.text: The Aesir sent messengers through all the world to bid everything weep Baldr out of Hel; and all things did - men and every living creature, the earth, the stones, the trees, and all metals, as you may see these things weep when they come from frost into heat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 49 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: But at last they came to a giantess who called herself Thokk, sitting in a cave; she refused: 'Thokk will weep dry tears for Baldr's burial; let Hel hold what it has.' And men believe that this Thokk was Loki himself, who has done the greatest evil among gods and men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 49 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
